He passed away on March 12, 1985, at the age of 73, in Bangkok, after a prolonged illness. His funeral was attended by dignitaries, including former military leaders and politicians, reflecting his enduring legacy in Thai politics and society.

Throughout his life, Tappaya Sit-Or navigated the complexities of Thailand’s military and political spheres, leaving a mark as both a soldier and a statesman. His career reflected the turbulent nature of Thai politics in the mid-20th century, and his contributions to regional development ensured his lasting influence in southern Thailand.

title: Lokesh Kanagaraj
text:
Lokesh Kanagaraj was born on March 14, 1986, in Kinathukadavu, a small town in the Coimbatore district of Tamil Nadu, India. He grew up in a middle-class family, with his father working as a government employee and his mother as a homemaker. From a young age, Lokesh developed a keen interest in cinema, particularly Tamil films, which were a significant part of his upbringing. He completed his schooling at St. Joseph’s Matriculation Higher Secondary School in Kinathukadavu before pursuing a Bachelor of Engineering in Computer Science at the PSG College of Technology in Coimbatore, graduating in 2007.

After completing his engineering degree, Lokesh initially worked as a software engineer at Cognizant Technology Solutions in Chennai. However, his passion for filmmaking never waned. In 2011, he decided to pursue his dream and enrolled in the Film and Television Institute of Tamil Nadu (FTIT) in Chennai, where he studied direction and screenplay writing. During his time at FTIT, he honed his skills and developed a deep understanding of storytelling, cinematography, and editing. His student short films, such as *Aviyal* (2011), showcased his talent and earned him recognition in local film circles.

Lokesh’s professional breakthrough came in 2016 when he made his directorial debut with the short film *Aviyal*, which was part of an anthology of the same name. The film, produced by Karthik Subbaraj under his banner Stone Bench Creations, featured a nonlinear narrative and a gritty, realistic style that set it apart from conventional Tamil cinema. The anthology received critical acclaim, and Lokesh’s segment was particularly praised for its tight scripting and innovative storytelling. This success opened doors for him in the Tamil film industry.

In 2017, Lokesh made his feature film debut with *Maanagaram*, a crime thriller set in Chennai. The film, produced by Dream Warrior Pictures and starring Sundeep Kishan, Regina Cassandra, and Sri, was released on March 10, 2017. *Maanagaram* was a critical and commercial success, earning praise for its fast-paced narrative, realistic portrayal of urban life, and strong performances. The film’s budget was approximately ₹5 crore, and it grossed over ₹15 crore at the box office, establishing Lokesh as a promising director in Tamil cinema. His ability to weave multiple storylines into a cohesive whole was particularly noted by critics.

Following the success of *Maanagaram*, Lokesh directed *Kaithi* in 2019, a high-octane action thriller starring Karthi in the lead role. The film, produced by Dream Warrior Pictures and co-produced by Vijay Sethupathi, was released on October 25, 2019. *Kaithi* was a massive hit, both critically and commercially, with its gripping screenplay, intense action sequences, and Karthi’s powerhouse performance. Made on a budget of around ₹25 crore, the film grossed over ₹100 crore worldwide, becoming one of the highest-grossing Tamil films of the year. It also won several awards, including the Filmfare Award for Best Action and the Ananda Vikatan Cinema Award for Best Director.

Lokesh’s next project was *Master* (2021), a mass action drama starring Vijay and Vijay Sethupathi. The film, produced by Xavier Britto under his banner XB Film Creators, was released on January 13, 2021, during the Pongal festival. Despite the challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, *Master* became a blockbuster, grossing over ₹300 crore worldwide. While the film received mixed reviews for its pacing, Lokesh’s direction and the performances of the lead actors were widely appreciated. The film’s success further cemented his reputation as one of Tamil cinema’s most bankable directors.

In 2022, Lokesh returned with *Vikram*, a high-stakes action thriller starring Kamal Haasan, Vijay Sethupathi, and Fahadh Faasil. The film, produced by Raaj Kamal Films International, was released on June 3, 2022, and became a cultural phenomenon. *Vikram* was praised for its stylish action sequences, intricate plot, and powerful performances, particularly by Kamal Haasan. Made on a budget of ₹120 crore, the film grossed over ₹500 crore worldwide, making it one of the highest-grossing Tamil films of all time. It also won multiple awards, including the National Film Award for Best Action Direction and the Filmfare Award for Best Film.

As of 2024, Lokesh Kanagaraj continues to be a dominant force in Tamil cinema. He is currently working on *Thalaivar 171*, a highly anticipated film starring Rajinikanth, which is expected to release in 2025. Known for his meticulous planning, innovative storytelling, and ability to blend commercial appeal with artistic integrity, Lokesh has carved a unique niche for himself in the industry. His films are characterized by their fast-paced narratives, strong character arcs, and high-octane action sequences, making him one of the most sought-after directors in Indian cinema today. Despite his rapid rise to fame, he remains grounded and continues to push the boundaries of Tamil filmmaking.

title: Karni Liddell
text:
Karni Liddell was born on August 21, 1979, in Brisbane, Queensland, Australia, to parents Geoff and Robyn Liddell. She was diagnosed with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type 2 at just nine months old, a progressive neuromuscular condition that weakens muscles over time. Despite the challenges posed by her disability, Liddell grew up in a supportive family environment that encouraged her to pursue her passions. She attended local schools in Brisbane, including St. Joseph’s Nudgee College, where she completed her secondary education.

From an early age, Liddell demonstrated a strong interest in sports, particularly swimming. Though her condition limited her physical mobility, she began competitive swimming at the age of eight, training under coach Laurie Lawrence, a renowned Australian swim coach. Her determination and skill quickly became evident, and by the age of 12, she had set multiple national records in para-swimming events. In 1994, at just 15 years old, Liddell made her international debut at the IPC Swimming World Championships in Malta, where she won a silver medal in the 50-meter freestyle S6 classification.

Liddell’s career reached its peak at the 1996 Atlanta Paralympic Games, where she represented Australia at the age of 16. Competing in four events—the 50m freestyle, 100m freestyle, 400m freestyle, and 100m backstroke—she won two silver medals in the 50m and 100m freestyle S6 categories. Her performances earned her widespread recognition, and she was named Queensland Young Australian of the Year in 1997 for her achievements in sport and advocacy. Over the next few years, she continued to compete at a high level, including at the 1998 IPC World Championships in Christchurch, New Zealand, where she added more medals to her collection.

Beyond swimming, Liddell became a prominent advocate for disability rights and inclusion. In 1999, she was appointed as an ambassador for the Queensland Disability Advisory Council, where she worked to promote accessibility and equal opportunities for people with disabilities. Her advocacy extended to public speaking, where she shared her experiences to inspire others. In 2000, she was selected as one of the final torchbearers for the Sydney Paralympic Games, a moment that highlighted her role as a symbol of resilience and determination.

After retiring from competitive swimming in the early 2000s, Liddell transitioned into media and public relations. She worked as a presenter for the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) and contributed to various disability-focused programs. In 2004, she co-hosted the television series *No Limits*, a show that explored the lives of people with disabilities, further cementing her role as a public figure in the disability community. She also pursued higher education, earning a Bachelor of Communications from the University of the Sunshine Coast in 2005.

In her later years, Liddell remained active in advocacy and public life. She served on the board of Disability Services Australia and was a vocal supporter of the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS). In 2016, she was awarded the Medal of the Order of Australia (OAM) for her service to people with disabilities and her contributions to sport. She also continued her involvement in sports administration, working with organizations like Swimming Australia to promote inclusive programs.

Liddell’s personal life included her marriage to long-time partner, David, in 2010. The couple settled in Queensland, where she balanced her professional commitments with family life. Throughout her career, she remained a powerful voice for disability rights, using her platform to challenge stereotypes and push for greater inclusion in all aspects of society. As of 2024, she continues to be an influential figure in Australia, advocating for change and inspiring others through her story of perseverance and success.

title: Ronaldinho
text:
Ronaldinho, born Ronaldo de Assis Moreira on March 21, 1980, in Porto Alegre, Brazil, is widely regarded as one of the most skillful and entertaining footballers in history. His early life was marked by both tragedy and talent. The youngest of three children in a working-class family, Ronaldinho grew up in the Vila Nova neighborhood, where his father, João Moreira, worked as a shipyard welder and played amateur football for a local club. His mother, Miguelina de Assis, was a saleswoman who later became a nurse. Tragedy struck when Ronaldinho was just eight years old; his father drowned in the family’s swimming pool after suffering a heart attack on January 2, 1989. This loss deeply affected him, but football became his refuge.

Ronaldinho’s talent was evident from childhood. At age seven, he joined the youth academy of local club Grêmio Foot-Ball Porto Alegrense, where his older brother Roberto had also played. His precocious skills—dribbling, creativity, and an infectious smile—earned him the nickname "Ronaldinho," meaning "little Ronaldo," to distinguish him from the then-famous Brazilian striker Ronaldo Nazário. By age 13, he was already making headlines; in a youth tournament in 1993, he scored 23 goals in a single match, a 23-0 victory. His professional debut for Grêmio came on February 4, 1998, at age 17, in a Campeonato Gaúcho match against Internacional. Though Grêmio lost 1-0, Ronaldinho’s performance hinted at his future greatness.

His breakthrough came in 1999 when he led Grêmio to the Copa Sul-Minas title and was named the tournament’s best player. That same year, he made his debut for the Brazilian national team on June 26, 1999, in a 3-0 win over Latvia, scoring one goal. His dazzling displays, including a memorable performance at the 1999 Copa América, where Brazil won the tournament and he was named player of the tournament, caught the attention of European clubs. In 2001, at age 21, he signed with Paris Saint-Germain (PSG) for a reported fee of €5 million, though contractual disputes delayed his debut until August 4, 2001, in a Ligue 1 match against Auxerre.

Ronaldinho’s time at PSG (2001-2003) was mixed. While he showcased his brilliance—such as his two-goal performance in a 3-1 win over rivals Marseille in 2002—he also struggled with inconsistency and off-field distractions. Despite this, he helped Brazil win the 2002 FIFA World Cup in South Korea and Japan, though he was not a starter, playing a key role off the bench in the 2-1 quarterfinal victory over England, where he scored a free-kick and set up the winning goal. His crowning moment came in 2003 when he joined FC Barcelona for €30 million, a move that would define his career.

At Barcelona (2003-2008), Ronaldinho reached his peak. In his first season, he scored 15 goals in La Liga and was instrumental in reviving the club’s fortunes, leading them to a second-place finish after years of mediocrity. The 2004-05 season was his masterpiece: he scored 21 goals, provided 15 assists, and led Barcelona to their first La Liga title in six years. His performances earned him the FIFA World Player of the Year award in both 2004 and 2005, as well as the Ballon d’Or in 2005. Memorable moments included his solo goal against Chelsea in the 2004-05 Champions League, where he dribbled past multiple defenders, and his iconic "toothless" smile after nutmegging Real Madrid’s defender in a 3-0 *Clásico* victory at the Santiago Bernabéu in November 2005, a match where he received a standing ovation from the home fans.

Ronaldinho’s later years saw a decline in form and fitness. After leaving Barcelona in 2008, he joined AC Milan for €21 million, where he won the Serie A title in 2010-11, though he was no longer the dominant force of his prime. He returned to Brazil in 2011, playing for Flamengo, where he won the Campeonato Carioca in 2011, and later Atlético Mineiro, leading them to the 2013 Copa Libertadores title, their first in history. His final professional club was Fluminense in 2015, though he played only nine matches before leaving.

Internationally, Ronaldinho earned 97 caps for Brazil, scoring 33 goals. Beyond the 2002 World Cup, he won the 2005 FIFA Confederations Cup, where he was named player of the tournament, and the 2007 Copa América. His last major tournament was the 2008 Beijing Olympics, where Brazil won a bronze medal.

After retiring in 2015, Ronaldinho’s life took a turn. He became a global ambassador for football, appearing in exhibitions and charity matches. However, legal troubles marred his later years. In 2020, he and his brother Roberto were arrested in Paraguay for using fake passports and spent four months in prison before being released in August 2020. Despite these setbacks, he remains a beloved figure in football, celebrated for his joy, creativity, and unmatched skill. As of 2024, he lives in Brazil, occasionally appearing at football events and working as a brand ambassador. His legacy as one of the game’s greatest entertainers is secure.

title: Rana Sanaullah
text:
Rana Sanaullah Khan, a prominent Pakistani politician and lawyer, was born on January 1, 1955, in Faisalabad, Punjab, Pakistan. He hails from a politically active family, with his father, Rana Mohammad Shafqat Khan, having served as a member of the Provincial Assembly of Punjab. Sanaullah received his early education at Government College Faisalabad (now Government College University) before pursuing a law degree at the University of the Punjab in Lahore. He completed his LLB in 1978 and later enrolled as an advocate in the Lahore High Court in 1980, establishing a legal practice in Faisalabad.

Sanaullah’s political career began in the 1980s when he joined the Pakistan Muslim League (PML), a party with strong roots in Punjab. He initially contested local elections and gradually rose through the ranks. In 1988, he was elected as a member of the Provincial Assembly of Punjab for the first time, representing the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) faction, which had split from the original PML. His constituency was PP-58 (Faisalabad-VIII), and he won the seat with a significant margin, securing 28,124 votes against his closest rival’s 12,456. This victory marked the beginning of his long association with the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N), led by Nawaz Sharif.

Throughout the 1990s, Sanaullah remained an active legislator, serving multiple terms in the Punjab Assembly. He was re-elected in 1990, 1993, and 1997, each time from the same constituency. His political influence grew as he took on key roles within the PML-N, including serving as the Provincial Minister for Law and Parliamentary Affairs in Punjab from 1997 to 1999 under Chief Minister Shahbaz Sharif. During this period, he played a crucial role in shaping legal and administrative policies in the province, including efforts to streamline judicial appointments and improve governance.

After General Pervez Musharraf’s military coup in 1999, Sanaullah, like many PML-N leaders, faced political repression. He was arrested multiple times between 2000 and 2002 under charges of corruption and misuse of authority, though he maintained that these were politically motivated. Despite the crackdown, he remained loyal to the PML-N and contested the 2002 general elections from NA-79 (Faisalabad-V), losing to a candidate from the pro-Musharraf Pakistan Muslim League (Quaid-e-Azam). However, he made a strong comeback in the 2008 general elections, winning both the National Assembly seat (NA-79) and the Provincial Assembly seat (PP-58). He chose to retain his National Assembly seat and was appointed as the Federal Minister for Law, Justice, and Human Rights in the coalition government led by the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP), serving from March 2008 to February 2009.

Sanaullah’s tenure as Law Minister was marked by efforts to reform the judicial system, including the restoration of deposed judges following the 2007 lawyers' movement. He played a key role in negotiating the reinstatement of Chief Justice Iftikhar Muhammad Chaudhry and other judges who had been removed by Musharraf. However, his time in office was short-lived, as the PML-N withdrew from the coalition in 2009 over disagreements with the PPP on judicial appointments.

In the 2013 general elections, Sanaullah was re-elected to the National Assembly from NA-79 with 104,876 votes, defeating his closest rival by a margin of over 40,000 votes. He was subsequently appointed as the Federal Minister for Interior in the PML-N government led by Nawaz Sharif, serving from June 2013 to July 2017. As Interior Minister, he oversaw national security policies, counterterrorism operations, and law enforcement reforms. His tenure saw the launch of Operation Zarb-e-Azb in 2014, a military offensive against militant groups in North Waziristan, which significantly reduced terrorist attacks in Pakistan. He also played a role in managing the 2014 sit-in protests by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) and Pakistan Awami Tehreek (PAT) in Islamabad, which demanded the resignation of the government.

After Nawaz Sharif’s disqualification in 2017 following the Panama Papers case, Sanaullah remained a vocal defender of the PML-N’s leadership. He contested the 2018 general elections from NA-106 (Faisalabad-VI) but lost to a PTI candidate, marking a rare electoral defeat in his career. Despite this setback, he continued to serve as a senior leader of the PML-N, often appearing in media as a party spokesperson. In 2020, he was arrested by the Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF) on charges of drug trafficking, a case that he and the PML-N dismissed as politically motivated. He was released on bail in 2021 after spending nearly a year in detention.

Following the ouster of Imran Khan’s government in April 2022, Sanaullah was appointed as the Federal Minister for Interior once again in the coalition government led by Shehbaz Sharif. He took office on April 19, 2022, and remained in the position until the dissolution of the National Assembly in August 2023. During this tenure, he oversaw security arrangements for the 2023 general elections and dealt with challenges such as rising political polarization and militant threats. After the PML-N’s return to power in 2024, he was reappointed as Interior Minister in the cabinet of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, a position he continues to hold as of mid-2024.

Throughout his career, Rana Sanaullah has been a polarizing figure, admired by supporters for his political resilience and criticized by opponents for alleged corruption and authoritarian tendencies. Despite controversies, he remains one of the most influential politicians in Punjab and a key strategist for the PML-N. His legal background, political experience, and close association with the Sharif family have cemented his role as a central figure in Pakistan’s political landscape.

title: Chris Duffield
text:
Chris Duffield was born on October 12, 1952, in Sheffield, South Yorkshire, England. He grew up in a working-class family, the son of a steelworker father and a homemaker mother. From an early age, Duffield showed an aptitude for leadership and public service, influenced by his parents' strong work ethic and community values. He attended local schools in Sheffield, including King Edward VII School, where he excelled academically and participated in student government. After completing his secondary education in 1970, he enrolled at the University of Leeds, where he studied politics and economics, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1973.

Duffield began his professional career in local government, joining Sheffield City Council in 1974 as a trainee administrative officer. His early roles involved urban planning and housing policy, areas that would later define much of his career. By 1978, he had risen to the position of principal officer in the housing department, overseeing major regeneration projects in the city’s deprived neighborhoods. His work during this period earned him recognition for his pragmatic approach to social housing, particularly in the wake of the 1980s economic downturn, which hit Sheffield’s industrial base hard.

In 1985, Duffield moved to London to take up a senior role at the Association of Metropolitan Authorities (AMA), a national body representing local government interests. As head of housing and urban policy, he played a key role in shaping legislation during Margaret Thatcher’s government, advocating for greater investment in public housing despite the prevailing political climate favoring privatization. His efforts contributed to the preservation of council housing stock at a time when many local authorities were selling off properties under the Right to Buy scheme. By 1990, he had become the AMA’s deputy chief executive, a position he held until the organization merged with other local government associations in 1997 to form the Local Government Association (LGA).

Duffield’s most prominent role came in 2001, when he was appointed chief executive of the London Borough of Hammersmith and Fulham, one of the capital’s most high-profile local authorities. During his tenure, which lasted until 2011, he oversaw a period of significant transformation. The borough, which included affluent areas like Fulham and more deprived neighborhoods such as White City, faced complex challenges, including housing shortages, regeneration demands, and the 2012 London Olympics preparations. Under his leadership, Hammersmith and Fulham secured £1.2 billion in private investment for the redevelopment of White City, creating thousands of new homes and jobs. He also introduced cost-saving measures that reduced the council’s budget deficit by 30% within three years, earning praise from both political allies and opponents.

Beyond his executive roles, Duffield was a respected figure in public administration circles. He served as president of the Society of Local Authority Chief Executives (SOLACE) from 2008 to 2010, where he advocated for greater devolution of powers to local government. He was also a visiting lecturer at the University of Birmingham’s Institute of Local Government Studies, where he taught courses on urban policy and public sector management. His contributions to local government were recognized in 2010 when he was awarded an Order of the British Empire (OBE) for services to public administration.

After retiring from Hammersmith and Fulham in 2011, Duffield remained active in consultancy and advisory roles. He founded Duffield Public Sector Consulting, which provided strategic advice to local authorities and housing associations across the UK. His clients included the Greater London Authority and several metropolitan councils, where he advised on regeneration projects and financial sustainability. He also served as a non-executive director for the housing association Peabody Trust from 2012 to 2018, helping to guide its expansion in London and the Southeast.

In his later years, Duffield divided his time between London and his home in the Peak District, where he enjoyed hiking and volunteering with local conservation groups. He remained a vocal commentator on local government issues, writing articles for publications such as *The Municipal Journal* and speaking at conferences. Despite his retirement, he continued to mentor young professionals in public administration, emphasizing the importance of ethical leadership and community-focused governance. Chris Duffield passed away on March 15, 2023, at the age of 70, following a brief illness. His legacy endures in the policies and projects he championed, which continue to shape urban development and public service in the UK.

title: Ted Mack (politician)
text:
Ted Mack was an Australian politician and independent member of the New South Wales Legislative Assembly and the Australian House of Representatives, known for his principled stance against party politics and his advocacy for democratic reform. Born Edward Charles Mack on 26 August 1933 in Sydney, New South Wales, he grew up in the working-class suburb of Marrickville. His father, Charles Mack, was a tram driver, and his mother, Ethel Mack, worked in a clothing factory. Mack attended Marrickville Public School and later Fort Street High School, one of Sydney’s selective public schools, where he developed an early interest in politics and public service.

After completing his secondary education, Mack enrolled at the University of Sydney, graduating with a Bachelor of Architecture in 1957. He worked as an architect in both the public and private sectors, including a period with the New South Wales Government Architect’s Office in the 1960s. His professional career was marked by a commitment to urban planning and public housing, issues that would later influence his political work. In 1960, he married Judith Ann Smith, with whom he had three children: David, Peter, and Catherine.

Mack’s political career began in local government. In 1974, at the age of 41, he was elected as an independent alderman on North Sydney Council, a position he held until 1980. During his time on the council, he gained a reputation for challenging established practices, particularly in planning and development. He opposed large-scale commercial projects that he believed prioritised profit over community needs, earning both admiration and criticism. His efforts to increase transparency in council decision-making and his advocacy for affordable housing made him a prominent figure in local politics.

In 1981, Mack ran for the New South Wales Legislative Assembly as an independent candidate for the seat of North Shore, which covered much of Sydney’s lower north shore. He won the seat in a by-election on 19 September 1981, defeating the Liberal Party candidate, John McLaughlin, with 52.4% of the vote after preferences. His victory was significant, as it marked the first time an independent had won a state seat in New South Wales in over 30 years. As a member of parliament, Mack continued his advocacy for democratic reform, including fixed four-year terms for the Legislative Assembly and the introduction of citizen-initiated referendums. He also opposed the privatisation of public assets and campaigned for better public transport and environmental protections.

Mack held the North Shore seat until 1988, when he resigned to contest the federal seat of North Sydney in the Australian House of Representatives. He won the seat in the 1990 federal election, defeating the Liberal incumbent, John Spender, with 56.5% of the two-party-preferred vote. His victory was part of a broader wave of support for independents and minor parties in that election, which saw the Australian Democrats and other crossbenchers gain influence. In federal parliament, Mack remained a vocal critic of party discipline, arguing that it stifled independent thought and accountability. He introduced several private member’s bills, including one in 1992 proposing a national integrity commission, a concept that would later gain widespread support.

One of Mack’s most notable achievements was his role in the formation of the Charter of Budget Honesty Act 1998, which required the federal government to provide independent economic forecasts and costings for election promises. He also advocated for electoral reform, including the introduction of proportional representation for the House of Representatives. Despite his independent status, he often worked with other crossbenchers to hold the major parties to account, particularly on issues of transparency and accountability.

Mack retired from federal politics in 1996, choosing not to contest the election that year. His decision was influenced by his belief that politicians should serve limited terms to prevent the entrenchment of power. After leaving parliament, he remained active in public life, serving on various boards and committees, including the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) Board from 1996 to 2000. He also continued to advocate for democratic reform, writing and speaking on issues such as electoral integrity and the need for greater citizen participation in government.

In his later years, Mack lived in Sydney with his wife, Judith. He remained a respected figure in Australian politics, often cited as an example of principled independence in a system dominated by party politics. Ted Mack died on 22 March 2018 at the age of 84, following a battle with cancer. His legacy endures in the reforms he championed and the example he set as a politician who prioritised integrity and public service over party loyalty.

title: Kubota Beisen
text:
Kubota Beisen, born Kubota Kinnosuke on March 15, 1852, in Kyoto, Japan, was a prominent painter, illustrator, and art educator of the Meiji era. His early life was shaped by the cultural and political upheavals of the time, as Japan transitioned from the feudal Tokugawa shogunate to the modernizing Meiji government. Beisen’s family was originally from the samurai class, serving the Toyotomi clan before their downfall in 1615. His father, Kubota Beishō, was a minor government official and amateur painter, which exposed young Kinnosuke to art from an early age.

At the age of 12, in 1864, Beisen began formal training in painting under the guidance of the renowned artist Mori Kansai, a master of the Shijō school, which blended traditional Japanese techniques with Chinese influences. This apprenticeship lasted for over a decade, during which Beisen honed his skills in ink painting, figure drawing, and landscape composition. By the late 1870s, he had adopted the art name "Beisen," derived from his father’s pseudonym, and began establishing himself as an independent artist.

In 1877, at the age of 25, Beisen participated in the first National Industrial Exhibition in Tokyo, where his work caught the attention of government officials and art patrons. This exposure led to his appointment as an instructor at the Kyoto Prefectural School of Painting in 1880, a position he held for nearly two decades. During this time, he played a key role in modernizing Japanese art education, incorporating Western techniques such as perspective and shading while maintaining traditional Japanese aesthetics. His students included notable artists like Takeuchi Seihō and Kikuchi Hōbun, who would later become central figures in the Nihonga movement.

Beisen’s career reached new heights in the 1890s when he was commissioned to document Japan’s military campaigns. In 1894, during the First Sino-Japanese War, he was embedded with the Imperial Japanese Army as an official war artist, producing a series of detailed sketches and paintings that depicted battles, soldiers, and the landscapes of Korea and China. These works were later published in the illustrated book *Nisshin Sensō Jikki* (True Record of the Sino-Japanese War, 1895), which included 100 of his illustrations. His war art was notable for its realism and dynamic composition, blending traditional Japanese brushwork with Western-style reportage.

Beyond his war illustrations, Beisen was a prolific painter of historical and genre scenes. His 1897 work *The Battle of Yashima*, depicting a 12th-century naval conflict between the Taira and Minamoto clans, showcased his mastery of large-scale narrative painting. He also contributed to the development of *ukiyo-e* (woodblock prints) in the Meiji era, collaborating with publishers like Yamada Naoemon to produce prints of famous warriors and beauties. In 1898, he was appointed to the Imperial Art Committee, a government body tasked with promoting Japanese art both domestically and abroad.

In his later years, Beisen continued to teach and paint while also engaging in cultural diplomacy. In 1900, he traveled to Paris as part of the Japanese delegation to the Exposition Universelle, where his work was exhibited alongside that of other leading Japanese artists. His paintings, which included scenes of Japanese life and history, were well received by European audiences. Upon returning to Japan, he focused on refining his style, often depicting themes of nature and classical literature.

Beisen’s health began to decline in the early 1900s, and he retired from teaching in 1906. He spent his final years in Kyoto, where he continued to paint and mentor younger artists. Kubota Beisen died on April 19, 1906, at the age of 54, due to complications from diabetes. He was buried in Kyoto’s Tōfuku-ji Temple, a site traditionally associated with artists and scholars. Throughout his career, Beisen produced an estimated 2,000 paintings and illustrations, leaving a lasting legacy as a bridge between traditional Japanese art and the modernizing influences of the Meiji era. His works are preserved in collections such as the Kyoto National Museum and the Tokyo National Museum, ensuring his place in Japan’s artistic history.

title: Daniil Medvedev
text:
Daniil Sergeyevich Medvedev was born on February 11, 1996, in Moscow, Russia, to parents Sergey Medvedev, a computer engineer, and Olga Medvedeva, a homemaker. From an early age, Medvedev showed an aptitude for sports, initially trying his hand at ice hockey and football before settling on tennis at the age of six. His parents recognized his potential and enrolled him in the Sport School of Olympic Reserve No. 2 in Moscow, where he trained under coach Ekaterina Kryuchkova. At the age of 12, Medvedev switched to the renowned tennis academy of former professional player Jean-René Lisnard in Antibes, France, where he spent several formative years refining his skills.

Medvedev turned professional in 2014 at the age of 18, competing in Futures and Challenger tournaments to build his ranking. His breakthrough came in 2016 when he won his first ATP Challenger title in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, France, in September, followed by another Challenger victory in Rennes later that year. These successes propelled him into the top 200 of the ATP rankings for the first time. In 2017, Medvedev made his Grand Slam debut at Wimbledon, where he reached the second round before losing to Ruben Bemelmans. That same year, he claimed his first ATP Tour title at the Winston-Salem Open in August, defeating Steve Johnson in the final. By the end of 2017, his ranking had climbed to No. 65 in the world.

The 2018 season marked Medvedev’s emergence as a consistent force on the ATP Tour. He reached four finals that year, winning his second career title at the Sydney International in January and his third at the Winston-Salem Open in August. His most significant achievement came at the US Open, where he advanced to the fourth round, defeating Stefanos Tsitsipas before falling to eventual champion Novak Djokovic. Medvedev finished the year ranked No. 16, a career-high at the time. His 2019 campaign solidified his status as one of tennis’s rising stars. He won four titles, including his first Masters 1000 crown at the Cincinnati Open in August, where he defeated David Goffin in the final. At the US Open, Medvedev reached his first Grand Slam final, losing a grueling five-set match to Rafael Nadal. Despite the defeat, his performance earned him widespread acclaim, and he ended the year ranked No. 5.

Medvedev’s peak came in 2021, a year that saw him ascend to the pinnacle of men’s tennis. He began the season by winning the ATP Cup with Team Russia, defeating Italy’s Matteo Berrettini in the final. In March, he claimed his second Masters 1000 title at the Miami Open, defeating Jannik Sinner in the final. His crowning achievement arrived at the US Open in September, where he defeated Novak Djokovic in straight sets to win his first Grand Slam title, preventing Djokovic from completing the calendar-year Grand Slam. Medvedev became the first Russian man to win a Grand Slam since Marat Safin in 2005 and the first player outside the "Big Three" (Federer, Nadal, Djokovic) to win a major since Stan Wawrinka in 2016. Following his US Open triumph, Medvedev reached the world No. 1 ranking on February 28, 2022, becoming the first man outside the Big Three to hold the top spot since Andy Roddick in 2004.

In 2022, Medvedev continued to perform at an elite level, reaching the final of the Australian Open in January, where he lost to Rafael Nadal in another five-set epic. He also won four ATP titles that year, including the Vienna Open and the Rotterdam Open. However, his 2023 season was disrupted by a hernia surgery in April, which sidelined him for two months. Despite the setback, he returned to win the Italian Open in May, his first title on clay, and reached the semifinals of the US Open later that year. By the end of 2023, Medvedev had amassed 20 ATP singles titles, including six Masters 1000 crowns, and had earned over $40 million in prize money.

Beyond tennis, Medvedev married his longtime girlfriend, Daria Chernyshkova, in 2018. The couple welcomed their first child, a daughter named Alisa, in October 2022. Known for his analytical approach to the game and his often reserved demeanor on court, Medvedev has become one of the most consistent players of his generation, frequently reaching deep into tournaments and challenging the dominance of the sport’s established stars. As of 2024, he remains a top contender in men’s tennis, with his sights set on adding more Grand Slam titles to his resume.

title: Nancy Onyango
text:
Nancy Onyango was born on October 10, 1961, in Kisumu, Kenya, a city in the western part of the country. She grew up in a modest family, with her parents emphasizing the importance of education from an early age. Onyango attended local primary and secondary schools in Kisumu before pursuing higher education. In 1980, she enrolled at the University of Nairobi, where she studied commerce, graduating in 1984 with a Bachelor of Commerce degree. Her academic performance was strong, and she developed a keen interest in finance and accounting, fields that would later define her career.

After completing her undergraduate studies, Onyango began her professional journey in the public sector. In 1985, she joined the Office of the Auditor-General in Kenya as an auditor, where she worked for five years. During this period, she gained valuable experience in financial oversight, auditing, and public sector accountability. Her work involved reviewing government expenditures and ensuring compliance with financial regulations, which laid the foundation for her future roles in governance and international finance.

In 1990, Onyango took a significant step in her career by moving to the United Kingdom to pursue further education. She enrolled at the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE), where she earned a Master of Science in Accounting and Finance in 1991. This advanced degree expanded her expertise and opened doors to international opportunities. Following her studies, she worked briefly in the UK, gaining exposure to global financial practices before returning to Kenya in the mid-1990s.

Upon her return, Onyango joined the private sector, working for PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) in Nairobi as a senior auditor. Her role involved auditing multinational corporations and advising on financial management, which further sharpened her skills in corporate governance and risk assessment. In 1998, she was appointed as the Director of Finance and Administration at the Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA), a critical position in Kenya’s tax administration. During her tenure, which lasted until 2003, she played a key role in modernizing the KRA’s financial systems, improving tax collection efficiency, and reducing corruption within the agency. Under her leadership, the KRA’s revenue collection increased significantly, contributing to Kenya’s economic stability.

In 2004, Onyango transitioned to the international stage when she joined the International Monetary Fund (IMF) as a Senior Financial Sector Expert. Based in Washington, D.C., she worked in the IMF’s African Department, focusing on financial sector reforms in sub-Saharan Africa. Her responsibilities included providing technical assistance to governments, assessing financial sector stability, and designing policies to strengthen banking systems. Over the next decade, she worked on projects in countries such as Nigeria, Ghana, Uganda, and Tanzania, helping to implement reforms that improved financial transparency and economic resilience.

One of Onyango’s most notable achievements came in 2014 when she was appointed as the Director of the IMF’s Office of Internal Audit and Inspection (OIA). In this role, she led a team responsible for evaluating the IMF’s internal controls, risk management, and governance processes. Her work ensured that the institution adhered to the highest standards of accountability and efficiency. She held this position until 2019, during which time she also served as a member of the IMF’s Executive Board, representing African countries.

Beyond her professional roles, Onyango has been actively involved in mentoring young professionals, particularly women in finance and governance. She has served on the boards of several organizations, including the Kenya Institute of Management and the African Capacity Building Foundation. In 2020, she retired from the IMF but remained engaged in advisory work, offering her expertise to governments and international organizations on financial sector reforms and public sector governance.

Nancy Onyango’s career is marked by a commitment to financial integrity, public service, and international development. Her contributions have had a lasting impact on Kenya’s financial systems and the broader African continent. As of 2024, she resides in the United States, where she continues to be involved in consultancy and advocacy for good governance and economic development. Her life and work serve as an inspiration to many, particularly women aspiring to leadership roles in finance and public administration.

title: Giorgi Papunashvili
text:
Giorgi Papunashvili was born on September 28, 1995, in Tbilisi, the capital of Georgia. From an early age, he showed a keen interest in football, a passion that would shape his future. His family, though not particularly involved in sports, supported his ambitions, and by the age of six, he was already training at a local youth academy. His early development took place at the Dinamo Tbilisi youth system, one of Georgia’s most prestigious football academies, where he honed his skills as a midfielder.

Papunashvili’s professional career began in 2012 when, at the age of 16, he made his debut for Dinamo Tbilisi’s senior team. His first appearance came on November 10, 2012, in a Georgian Erovnuli Liga match against FC Merani Martvili. Though his early playing time was limited, his technical ability and vision on the field quickly caught the attention of coaches and scouts. By the 2013-14 season, he had become a more regular fixture in the squad, contributing to Dinamo’s domestic success. That season, Dinamo won the Georgian Cup, with Papunashvili making several appearances, including in the final, which Dinamo won 2-1 against Chikhura Sachkhere on May 21, 2014.

His breakthrough season came in 2014-15, when he established himself as a key player for Dinamo Tbilisi. That year, he scored six goals in 28 league appearances, helping the team secure the Erovnuli Liga title. His performances earned him recognition as one of the league’s most promising young talents. In 2015, he was named the Georgian Football Federation’s Young Player of the Year, further solidifying his reputation. That same year, he made his debut for the Georgian national team, coming on as a substitute in a UEFA Euro 2016 qualifier against Scotland on October 8, 2015.

In January 2016, Papunashvili made a significant move to Europe, signing with Werder Bremen II, the reserve team of the German Bundesliga club Werder Bremen. The transfer was seen as a major step in his career, offering him the chance to develop in a more competitive environment. However, his time in Germany was challenging. He struggled to break into the first team, making only 12 appearances for Werder Bremen II in the Regionalliga Nord during the 2015-16 season. Despite the difficulties, the experience provided him with valuable exposure to European football.

After a year in Germany, Papunashvili returned to Georgia in early 2017, rejoining Dinamo Tbilisi. His second spell with the club was productive, as he helped Dinamo win another Erovnuli Liga title in the 2017 season. He scored five goals in 25 appearances that year, reaffirming his status as one of Georgia’s top midfielders. His performances also earned him a recall to the national team, where he became a more regular presence in the squad.

In July 2018, Papunashvili made another move abroad, this time to Poland, signing with Wisła Płock in the Ekstraklasa. His time in Poland was marked by steady progress, though he faced competition for playing time. Over two seasons, he made 40 league appearances, scoring three goals. His most notable performance came on August 18, 2018, when he scored a brace in a 3-2 win against Górnik Zabrze. Despite his efforts, Wisła Płock struggled in the league, and Papunashvili sought a new challenge in 2020.

That year, he joined FC Samtredia in Georgia, where he spent a brief period before moving to FC Saburtalo Tbilisi in 2021. His tenure at Saburtalo was short-lived, as he soon returned to Dinamo Tbilisi for a third spell in 2022. By this point, his career had entered a more stable phase, with Dinamo providing him a familiar environment to contribute. In the 2022 season, he made 20 league appearances, helping the team secure a third-place finish in the Erovnuli Liga.

Beyond his club career, Papunashvili has remained a consistent presence in the Georgian national team. As of 2024, he has earned over 20 caps, though he has yet to score for his country. His international career has included appearances in UEFA Nations League matches and World Cup qualifiers, where he has been valued for his work rate and passing ability.

In his later years, Papunashvili has focused on maintaining his fitness and contributing to Dinamo Tbilisi’s campaigns. While he has not reached the heights once predicted for him, he remains a respected figure in Georgian football. Off the field, he has kept a low profile, dedicating himself to his career and family. As of 2024, at the age of 28, he continues to play professionally, though his future in the sport remains uncertain as he approaches the latter stages of his career.

title: David Bogue
text:
David Bogue was born on February 18, 1750, in the small village of Hallydown, near Coldingham, Berwickshire, Scotland. His parents, David Bogue and Janet Turnbull, were farmers of modest means, and young Bogue received his early education at a local parish school. At the age of 14, he was apprenticed to a merchant in nearby Dunbar, but his academic inclinations led him to abandon commerce in favor of further study. In 1767, at 17, he enrolled at the University of Edinburgh, where he studied divinity under prominent theologians such as Hugh Blair and William Robertson. He graduated in 1771 with an MA, having distinguished himself in classical studies and moral philosophy.

After completing his university education, Bogue spent several years as a private tutor, first in Scotland and later in England. In 1776, he accepted a position as minister of the Independent (Congregational) church in Gosport, Hampshire, a role he would hold for the rest of his life. The Gosport congregation was small when he arrived, but under his leadership, it grew significantly, becoming one of the most influential dissenting churches in southern England. His preaching was noted for its clarity, depth, and evangelical fervor, attracting both local worshippers and visitors from further afield.

Bogue’s influence extended beyond his pulpit. In 1789, he co-founded the Gosport Theological Seminary with his friend and fellow minister, James Bennett. The seminary, established to train dissenting ministers, became a leading institution of its kind, producing over 300 graduates during its operation. Among its most notable alumni were Robert Morrison, the first Protestant missionary to China, and Thomas Chalmers, a key figure in the Scottish Free Church movement. Bogue himself taught theology, church history, and pastoral practice, emphasizing both academic rigor and practical ministry skills. The seminary operated until 1826, a year after Bogue’s death, when it merged with Highbury College in London.

In addition to his work in Gosport, Bogue was deeply involved in the broader evangelical movement. He was a founding member of the London Missionary Society (LMS) in 1795, which became one of the most significant missionary organizations of the 19th century. Bogue delivered the inaugural sermon at the society’s first meeting, held at the Castle and Falcon Inn in Aldersgate Street, London, on September 22, 1795. His address, later published as *A Sermon on the Duty of Promoting the Gospel Among the Heathen*, articulated the urgency of global evangelism and helped shape the society’s vision. The LMS went on to send missionaries to the South Pacific, Africa, and Asia, including figures like John Williams and David Livingstone.

Bogue was also a prolific writer. Between 1808 and 1812, he co-authored with James Bennett a four-volume work titled *A History of the Dissenters from the Revolution in 1688 to the Year 1808*. This comprehensive history, totaling over 2,000 pages, remains a key source for understanding the development of nonconformist Christianity in Britain. He contributed to other publications as well, including the *Evangelical Magazine*, and was known for his editorial work on religious periodicals.

Despite his many achievements, Bogue’s later years were marked by personal tragedy. His first wife, Mary Hay, whom he married in 1777, died in 1793, leaving him with several young children. He remarried in 1795 to Elizabeth Cogan, but she too passed away in 1811. Bogue himself suffered from declining health in his final years, though he remained active in ministry and writing until the end. He died on October 25, 1825, at the age of 75, in Gosport, where he was buried in the congregational churchyard. His legacy endured through the institutions he helped establish and the generations of ministers and missionaries he inspired. The London Missionary Society, in particular, continued its work for over two centuries, eventually merging into the Council for World Mission in 1977.
